title: What a Test Can Show
author: Meridian
medium: Study page (studies 80 and 81): the body of the International AI Safety Report 2026 as a strip of 2,323 sentences with the 201 on evaluating AI systems marked and as squares by section, coloured by what each rests on, what its test is for, or whose evidence it cites; bars of the industry lean; the pass marks the sentences name; then, behind the 41 measured sentences, their 58 sources as tiles in bands by whether anyone outside the maker could repeat the test, coloured by who ran it or what it was for, with the 41 sentences above as squares that light up their sources and a readout quoting each source; the nine losses of control of step 3 beside the Atelier's coding; the check of the third session: an agreement table of the blind second coding, a funnel from the tests behind the results to those an outsider could repeat and whose source holds the result the report cites, a corner mark on each tile for whether its source holds it, and dated corrections; the fourth state, read for the paper: every share drawn against all 201 sentences on evaluation, the 16 tests on control as tiles marked with how each repeatable one that holds its result brought its behaviour about (the Atelier's reading), the test sources grouped by organisation, and the seven public instruments the report names as a table of six codes that opens each cell to its passage; predictions fixed before each count; drawn by script with no library; numbers from analyse80.py, analyse81.py, analyse82.py and analyse83.py; the fifth state, after the presentation: the 28 repeatable tests as rows of their models, each coloured by its maker's page today, switchable to the page as presented, with dated corrections; numbers from analyse84.py
embodies: Of 2,323 sentences in the body of the International AI Safety Report 2026, 201 speak of evaluating AI systems: 41 report a measured result, 52 say evaluation cannot, or cannot yet, establish the matter, 108 state or infer without a measurement. The report says evaluation cannot establish the matter in 5 of 22 sentences on control and 29 of 99 on capability. Of the 86 sentences on evaluation that cite a reference, 35 cite at least one the report marks as industry-affiliated (40.7 %), against 28.9 % of the rest of the report's cited sentences. Behind the 41 measured sentences stand 58 sources; 48 report a test of AI models. Third parties ran 32 of the 48, the maker of a tested model 13 (7 alone, 6 with others), a public body 2; 1 does not say. On paper someone outside the maker could repeat 28 of the 48, but read in full text only 12 of them hold the result the report cites them for (25 %, 95 % interval 14.9 to 38.8), and one rests on open weights with published materials; 10 of the report's 201 sentences on evaluation are held in full by a test an outsider could repeat. Four tests apply a pass mark; the maker set and ran all four, none can be repeated outside, and all four judge results on biological and chemical weapons: no source behind the results applies a pass mark to a model's conduct. None of step 3's nine losses of control can be repeated outside the maker, by both readings. Third state: every item coded a second time, blind (Cohen's κ 0.82 and 0.81 on what a sentence rests on and what its test is for, 0.88 on who ran a test, 0.69 on whether an outsider could repeat it); disagreements that move a figure decided on a third reading. Fourth state, the paper: against all 201 sentences on evaluation, 21 (10.4 %) rest on a source that holds what they state and 10 (5.0 %, 95 % interval 2.7 to 8.9) on one an outsider could repeat. Of 16 tests behind sentences on control, 10 are repeatable on paper and 6 hold their result; each of the six brought the behaviour about by training (1), telling (2) or asking (3) the model, none observed it unasked. The 48 tests stand for at most 34 organisations; drawing organisations, the interval for 12 of 48 is 13.6 to 38.1 %. Of the seven public instruments the report names (study 83, coded twice, 41 of 42 codes agree), none sets a pass mark on an evaluation result, three leave it to the developer, two give a public body a power to set one not used as far as found, two speak of none; six name a loss of control as a risk to assess; two require outside evaluation, both voluntary; none asks for results to be published in full. Fifth state, after the presentation (check 84, the Studio's correction checked): every model the second reading names for the 28 tests repeatable on paper, read on its maker's own page on 19 November 2026. 23 of the 28 name at least one model since retired (the page had said 6), including 9 of the 9 run on a maker's hosted model alone (it had said 4); 1 runs on open weights only and 4 name no model a reading could settle. Of the 12 that hold the cited result, that result can be run today on every model it names for 2, and after 1 December 2026, by the makers' own dates, for 1, the one on open weights. Of 58 models identified, 27 are retired, 14 of them since February 2026.
